questions.question: What are generics in Java and why are they used?
questions.title: Java Generics Basics
questions.direct_answer: **Generics** let you parameterize types — e.g. `List<String>` — so the compiler enforces what goes in and out, giving **compile-time type safety** and removing manual casts. They turn runtime `ClassCastException`s into compile errors and make code reusable across types via type parameters like `<T>`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand generics provide compile-time safety and what problem they replaced
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying generics improve runtime performance, or not knowing pre-generics code needed casts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention type erasure: generics are a compile-time feature, erased to Object/bounds at runtime

sections.title: Type Safety Without Casts
sections.content:
**Generics** parameterize types so a collection or class knows the exact type it holds. `List<String>` is a list that can only contain `String`s; the compiler rejects anything else and lets you read elements without casting.

Before generics (pre-Java 5), collections held `Object`, so you had to cast on the way out and a wrong cast blew up at runtime with `ClassCastException`. Generics move that check to **compile time** — mistakes become compile errors instead of production crashes. They also enable **reusable** code: a single `Box<T>` or method `<T> T first(List<T>)` works for any type while staying type-safe. Note they're a compile-time feature: at runtime the type parameter is **erased** (more on that under type erasure).

sections.title: Why Generics Exist
sections.content:
blue|Type safety|~Compile-time checks|wrong type = compile error|no surprise ClassCastException|catches bugs early
emerald|No casts|~Cleaner reads|get returns the real type|no (String) casting|more readable
amber|Reusability|~Write once, use for any type|generic class Box of T|generic method first|same code, many types
rose|Type erasure|~Compile-time only|erased to Object/bound at runtime|no generic info in bytecode|why you can't do new T()

sections.title: Pre-generics: Object collections, casts, runtime crashes
With generics: the compiler enforces the type
Reusable Generic Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking generics speed up runtime.** They're compile-time safety; bytecode is the same after erasure.
- **Using raw types.** `List list = new ArrayList()` drops all safety and brings back casts.
- **Expecting runtime type info.** Because of erasure you can't do `new T()` or `instanceof T`.
- **Forgetting the diamond.** Use `new ArrayList<>()` (Java 7+) instead of repeating the type.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Generics = **parameterized types** (`List<String>`) for compile-time type safety.
- They **eliminate casts** and turn `ClassCastException`s into compile errors.
- Enable **reusable** generic classes and methods via `<T>`.
- They replaced pre-Java-5 `Object` collections that required manual casting.
- **Type erasure**: generic info is removed at runtime — a compile-time-only feature.
- Use the **diamond operator** `<>` to avoid repeating type arguments.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Generics let you parameterize types, so instead of a plain list you declare a List of String, and the compiler knows exactly what that list can hold. The main reason they exist is compile-time type safety. If I try to put an Integer into a List of String, that's a compile error, caught immediately, rather than a crash later. Before generics, which arrived in Java 5, collections just held Object. So you could put anything in, and when you read an element out you had to cast it back to the type you expected. If you cast wrong, you got a ClassCastException at runtime, often in production. Generics move that check from runtime to compile time, which is exactly where you want bugs caught. A second benefit is that you no longer need casts when reading — get returns the real type directly, so the code is cleaner. And a third benefit is reusability: I can write one generic class, like a Box of T, or a generic method, and it works for any type while staying type-safe, instead of duplicating code or falling back to Object. One important detail that impresses interviewers is type erasure. Generics are purely a compile-time feature. After compilation, the type parameter is erased — it becomes Object, or its bound — so there's no generic type information in the bytecode at runtime. That's why you can't write new T or use instanceof with a type parameter. So to sum up: generics give compile-time safety, remove casts, and enable reusable code, and they're implemented through erasure, not at runtime.

questions.question: What are raw types and why should you avoid them?
questions.title: Raw Types
questions.direct_answer: A **raw type** is a generic type used without its type parameter — e.g. `List` instead of `List<String>`. It exists only for backward compatibility with pre-generics code. Avoid it because it **disables compile-time type checking**, reintroduces unchecked casts, and can cause `ClassCastException` at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know raw types defeat generics and only exist for legacy compatibility
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing a raw type List with List<Object>, or not knowing it triggers unchecked warnings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note List<Object> is still type-checked, while raw List opts out of checking entirely

sections.title: Generics Turned Off
sections.content:
A **raw type** is a generic class or interface used without a type argument: `List` rather than `List<String>`. Raw types remain in the language only for **backward compatibility** with code written before generics (Java 5).

Using one effectively switches off generics: the compiler stops checking element types, you're back to casting, and the compiler emits an **unchecked warning** to flag the risk. A subtle but important distinction: `List<Object>` is *not* a raw type — it's fully type-checked and just happens to accept any object. A raw `List` opts out of checking entirely, which is why it's dangerous.

sections.title: Raw vs Parameterized vs Object
sections.content:
rose|Raw List|~Avoid|no type parameter|checking turned OFF|unchecked warnings
blue|List of String|~Preferred|fully type-checked|no casts needed|safe at compile time
emerald|List of Object|~Type-checked too|accepts any object|still safe|NOT a raw type
amber|Why raw exists|~Legacy only|backward compatibility|pre-Java-5 code|don't use in new code

sections.title: Raw type: checking off, runtime crash
Parameterized type: checking on, safe
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing raw `List` with `List<Object>`.** The latter is type-checked; the raw one isn't.
- **Ignoring unchecked warnings.** They're the compiler telling you type safety is off.
- **Using raw types to 'simplify'.** It only defers errors to runtime.
- **Mixing raw and generic APIs.** Passing a raw type can poison type inference and re-introduce casts.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A **raw type** is a generic used without its parameter (`List`, not `List<String>`).
- It exists only for **backward compatibility** with pre-generics code.
- Raw types **disable compile-time checking** and trigger **unchecked warnings**.
- `List<Object>` is **not** raw — it's fully type-checked.
- Raw types can cause `ClassCastException` at runtime.
- Always parameterize generic types in new code.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A raw type is a generic type used without its type parameter. So writing List instead of List of String, or Map instead of Map of String comma Integer — that's a raw type. They only still exist in the language for backward compatibility, so that code written before generics arrived in Java 5 still compiles. The problem is that using a raw type basically turns generics off. The compiler stops checking what you put into the collection, so you can mix a String and an Integer in the same list with no complaint at compile time. Then when you read elements out and cast them, you can get a ClassCastException at runtime — exactly the kind of bug generics were designed to prevent. The compiler does warn you with an unchecked warning, which is its way of saying type safety is no longer guaranteed here. One distinction that's worth calling out, because it trips people up, is that List of Object is not a raw type. List of Object is fully type-checked; it just happens to accept any object. The raw List, on the other hand, opts out of type checking entirely, and that's the dangerous part. So the bottom line is: always supply the type parameter in new code. If you genuinely need a collection of any object, use List of Object so you keep compile-time checking, and never fall back to a raw type just to silence the compiler.

questions.question: What are bounded wildcards in Java generics and when do you use them?
questions.title: Bounded Wildcards
questions.direct_answer: **Bounded wildcards** restrict an unknown type: `<? extends T>` is an **upper bound** (any subtype of T — read from it), `<? super T>` is a **lower bound** (any supertype of T — write to it). The **PECS** rule guides you: *Producer Extends, Consumer Super* — use `extends` when a structure produces values, `super` when it consumes them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand PECS and why you can't add to a List<? extends T>
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to add elements to a <? extends T> list, or confusing which bound allows reads vs writes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the read/write asymmetry: extends gives safe reads, super gives safe writes

sections.title: Upper and Lower Bounds
sections.content:
A **wildcard** `?` means 'some unknown type'. A **bounded** wildcard constrains it. `<? extends T>` is an **upper bound**: the type is T or a subtype, so you can safely **read** values as T — but you can't add (the compiler doesn't know the exact subtype). `<? super T>` is a **lower bound**: the type is T or a supertype, so you can safely **add** T values — but reads only give you `Object`.

This read/write asymmetry is summarized by **PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super**. If a parameter *produces* values you consume, use `extends`. If it *consumes* values you supply, use `super`. It makes generic APIs flexible: `List<? extends Number>` accepts `List<Integer>` or `List<Double>`.

sections.title: extends vs super (PECS)
sections.content:
blue|? extends T|~Upper bound|T or any subtype|safe to READ as T|cannot add (except null)
emerald|? super T|~Lower bound|T or any supertype|safe to WRITE T|reads give only Object
amber|PECS rule|~How to choose|Producer Extends|Consumer Super|matches read vs write
rose|Why no add to extends|~Compiler safety|exact subtype unknown|adding could break the list|null is the only safe add

sections.title: Trying to add to a producer (extends) — compile error
PECS in a copy method
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding to `<? extends T>`.** You can't (except `null`) — the exact subtype is unknown.
- **Reading useful types from `<? super T>`.** Reads only yield `Object`.
- **Reversing PECS.** Producer Extends, Consumer Super — mixing them up breaks the API.
- **Overusing wildcards.** For a method's own type relationships, a named type parameter `<T>` is often clearer.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `<? extends T>` = **upper bound**: read as T, can't add (producer).
- `<? super T>` = **lower bound**: add T, reads give Object (consumer).
- **PECS**: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
- `<? extends Number>` accepts `List<Integer>`, `List<Double>`, etc.
- Only `null` can be added to a `<? extends T>` collection.
- Wildcards make APIs flexible; named `<T>` suits internal type relations.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A wildcard, written as a question mark, means some unknown type, and a bounded wildcard puts a limit on it. There are two kinds. Question mark extends T is an upper bound — it means the type is T or some subtype of T. Because the type is at least a T, you can safely read values out as T. But you can't add anything, except null, because the compiler doesn't know the exact subtype, and adding the wrong thing could corrupt the collection. Question mark super T is a lower bound — the type is T or some supertype of T. That's the opposite situation: you can safely add T values, because a T fits into any supertype container, but when you read, all you're guaranteed is Object. The way to remember which to use is the PECS rule: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter produces values that you're going to read, use extends. If it consumes values that you're going to put in, use super. The classic example is a copy method: the source list produces elements, so it's a List of question mark extends T, and the destination consumes elements, so it's a List of question mark super T. That lets you copy a List of Integer into a List of Number, which is exactly the flexibility wildcards buy you. The most common mistake is trying to add to an extends list and being surprised it won't compile, and the second is reversing PECS. Just remember: extends for reading, super for writing.

questions.question: How do you write a generic class and a generic method in Java?
questions.title: Generic Classes and Methods
questions.direct_answer: A **generic class** declares a type parameter after the name: `class Box<T> { T value; }`. A **generic method** declares its own type parameter before the return type: `static <T> T first(List<T> list)`. The compiler **infers** `T` from the arguments, so callers rarely specify it explicitly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the syntax and where the type parameter goes for classes vs methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the <T> before the return type on a generic method, or thinking a generic method needs a generic class
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention type inference and bounded type parameters like <T extends Comparable<T>>

sections.title: Two Places Type Parameters Live
sections.content:
A **generic class** parameterizes the whole class: you write the type variable after the class name, `class Box<T>`, and use `T` for fields, parameters, and return types throughout the class. Every instance fixes `T` (e.g. `Box<String>`).

A **generic method** parameterizes a single method, independent of whether its class is generic. You declare the type variable **before the return type**: `static <T> T first(List<T> list)`. The compiler **infers** `T` from the call's arguments, so you usually just call `first(myList)`. You can also add **bounds**: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` restricts `T` to comparable types, letting you call `compareTo` inside the method.

sections.title: Generic Class vs Generic Method
sections.content:
blue|Generic class|~Parameterize the class|type variable after name: Box of T|use T for fields and methods|fixed per instance
emerald|Generic method|~Parameterize one method|type variable before return type|works in any class|inferred at the call site
amber|Bounds|~Restrict the type|T extends Comparable of T|enables calling bound methods|e.g. compareTo
rose|Type erasure limits|~Compile-time only|no new T|no T.class|no instanceof T

sections.title: Step 1: Write a Generic Class
sections.content:
Put the type parameter after the class name and use it inside:

| Part | Example |
|---|---|
| Declaration | `class Box<T> { ... }` |
| Field | `private T value;` |
| Method param | `void set(T value)` |
| Method return | `T get()` |
| Instantiation | `new Box<String>()` or `new Box<>()` |

sections.title: Step 2: Write a Generic Method
sections.content:
Declare the type parameter before the return type; the compiler infers it at the call site:

| Part | Example |
|---|---|
| Declaration | `static <T> T first(List<T> list)` |
| Bounded | `static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> l)` |
| Multiple params | `static <K, V> void put(K k, V v)` |
| Call (inferred) | `first(names)` |
| Call (explicit) | `Utils.<String>first(names)` |

sections.title: Generic Class and Method Together
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Missing `<T>` on a method.** A generic method needs the type parameter *before* the return type.
- **Assuming generic methods need a generic class.** A static generic method works in any class.
- **Trying `new T()`.** Type erasure means you can't instantiate a type parameter directly.
- **Skipping bounds.** Without `<T extends Comparable<T>>` you can't call `compareTo` on `T`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Generic class**: `class Box<T>` — type parameter after the class name.
- **Generic method**: `<T> T first(...)` — type parameter before the return type.
- The compiler **infers** `T` from arguments at the call site.
- **Bounds**: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` enable using the bound's methods.
- Multiple parameters allowed: `<K, V>`.
- Erasure prevents `new T()` and `T.class` at runtime.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: There are two different things here. A generic class parameterizes the entire class. You write the type variable in angle brackets right after the class name — class Box of T — and then you can use T anywhere inside: as a field type, a method parameter, or a return type. When you create an instance you fix the type, like Box of String, and from then on that box only holds Strings. A generic method parameterizes just one method, and importantly it doesn't require the class to be generic. The key syntax detail is where the type parameter goes: you declare it before the return type. So a method that returns the first element of a list looks like static, then angle bracket T, then T as the return type, then first, taking a List of T. The nice part is type inference — the compiler figures out what T is from the arguments you pass, so you just call first of myList and you don't have to specify the type yourself. You can also bound the type parameter. If I write angle bracket T extends Comparable of T, then T is restricted to types that implement Comparable, which lets me call compareTo on them inside the method — that's how you'd write a generic max method. The mistakes I'd watch for: forgetting the angle bracket T before the return type on a generic method, assuming a generic method needs a generic class when it doesn't, and trying to write new T, which doesn't work because of type erasure.
